solution:
$\Delta P\approx -D_{\text{mod}}\,\Delta y\,P=-1.8\times0.005\times950=-8.55$

title: Straddle Payoff at Expiry
prompt: A long straddle (long call and long put, both $K=\$50$, $T=0.5$ years) costs \$6. At expiry the stock is either \$55 or \$45. What is the straddle's payoff at expiry, before deducting the premium (round to 2 decimals)?
solution:
Straddle payoff $=\max(S_T-K,0)+\max(K-S_T,0)=|S_T-K|$.
$S_T=55$: payoff $=5$. $S_T=45$: payoff $=5$.
So the payoff is \$5.00 either way (the profit after the \$6 premium would be $-\$1$).

title: Duration–Convexity Price Change
prompt: A bond has modified duration 5 and convexity 20. Its yield rises by 1 percentage point. Using the duration–convexity approximation, estimate the percentage change in the bond's price (in %, round to 2 decimals).

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P}\approx -D\,\Delta y+\tfrac12 C(\Delta y)^2=-5(0.01)+\tfrac12(20)(0.01)^2=-0.05+0.001=-0.049$
So the price falls by about $4.90\%$.

title: Forward-Start Call
prompt: A stock (no dividends) trades at \$100. A forward-start call starts in 6 months: on that date its strike is set to 105% of the then stock price, and it expires 1 year after it starts. With $r=5\%$ and $\sigma=25\%$, what is its value today under Black–Scholes (round to 2 decimals)?
solution:
At the start date $t_1$ the option is an ordinary call with $K=1.05S_{t_1}$ and 1 year to run, worth $S_{t_1}\,c(1,1.05)$ by homogeneity of Black–Scholes. With no dividends, $S_{t_1}$ has present value $S_0$, so the value today is $S_0\,c(1,1.05)$, i.e. a BS call with $S=100$, $K=105$, $T=1$:
$d_1=\dfrac{\ln(100/105)+(0.05+0.03125)}{0.25}=0.1298,\ d_2=-0.1202$
$N(d_1)=0.5517,\ N(d_2)=0.4522$
$C=100(0.5517)-105e^{-0.05}(0.4522)=55.17-45.16=10.00$

subject: finance
title: Time Value of an American Call
prompt: An American call on a non-dividend-paying stock trades at \$5 and its intrinsic value is \$3. What is the option's time value, i.e. the amount you would give up by exercising now (round to 2 decimals)?
solution:
Time value $=$ price $-$ intrinsic $=5-3=\$2.00$.
For a non-dividend stock, early exercise of an American call is never optimal: exercising throws away this \$2.

Max profit $=(K_2-K_1)-\text{premium}=5-2=3.00$

title: Put Delta from a Market Price
prompt: A European put with $S=\$50$, $K=\$50$, $T=0.5$ years trades at \$2.00. The stock pays no dividends and $r=5\%$. Back out the Black–Scholes implied volatility, then compute the put's delta (round to 4 decimals).
solution:
Solve $P(\sigma)=Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2)-SN(-d_1)=2.00$ numerically (e.g. Newton or bisection): $\sigma_{\text{imp}}\approx18.46\%$.
Then $d_1=\dfrac{(0.05+0.1846^2/2)(0.5)}{0.1846\sqrt{0.5}}=0.2568$
$\Delta_P=N(d_1)-1=0.6013-1=-0.3987$

prompt: A stock (no dividends) trades at \$100. A forward-start call starts in 1 year: on that date its strike is set to 110% of the then stock price, and it then runs for 1 year. With $r=5\%$ and $\sigma=20\%$, value it today under Black–Scholes (round to 2 decimals).

By homogeneity, at the start date the option is worth $S_{t_1}c(1,1.10)$. With no dividends its value today is $S_0\,c(1,1.10)$: a BS call with $S=100$, $K=110$, $T=1$. The 1-year wait before it starts doesn't matter.

title: Minimum-Variance Weight
prompt: Two assets have variances $\sigma_1^2=0.04$, $\sigma_2^2=0.09$ and covariance $\sigma_{12}=0.01$ (expected returns 8% and 12%). Find the weight in asset 1 of the minimum-variance portfolio (round to 2 decimals).

$w_1^*=\dfrac{\sigma_2^2-\sigma_{12}}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2-2\sigma_{12}}=\dfrac{0.09-0.01}{0.04+0.09-0.02}=\dfrac{0.08}{0.11}=0.727\approx0.73$
(Expected returns don't affect the minimum-variance portfolio.)
